Bug_Title: Value-based classes should not be used for locking
Bug_Details:
According to the documentation,
A program may produce unpredictable results if it attempts to distinguish two references to equal values of a value-based class, whether directly
  via reference equality or indirectly via an appeal to synchronization…​
This is because value-based classes are intended to be wrappers for value types, which will be primitive-like collections of data (similar to struct s in other languages) that will come in future versions of Java.
Instances of a value-based class …​
do not have accessible constructors, but are instead instantiated through factory methods which make no commitment as to the identity of
    returned instances;
do not have accessible constructors, but are instead instantiated through factory methods which make no commitment as to the identity of
    returned instances;
This means that you can’t be sure you’re the only one trying to lock on any given instance of a value-based class, opening your code up to
contention and deadlock issues.
Under Java 8 breaking this rule may not actually break your code, but there are no guarantees of the behavior beyond that.
This rule raises an issue when a known value-based class is used for synchronization. That includes all the classes in the java.time package except Clock ; the date classes for alternate calendars, HijrahDate , JapaneseDate , MinguoDate , ThaiBuddhistDate ; and the optional classes: Optional , OptionalDouble , OptionalLong , OptionalInt .
Note that this rule is automatically disabled when the project’s sonar.java.source is lower than 8 .
Noncompliant code example
Optional<Foo> fOpt = doSomething();
synchronized (fOpt) {  // Noncompliant
  // ...
}
Bug_Explanation: The bug is embedded in the synchronized block where an Optional<Integer> is used as the lock object. According to the rule, value-based classes such as Optional should not be used for locking as their instances are not guaranteed to be unique.
Trigger_Explanation: The bug is triggered by creating two threads that try to synchronize on the same Optional instance. Since Optional is a value-based class, its instances are not guaranteed to be unique. This can lead to contention and deadlock issues.
